interviewQuestions.question: Why should a team treat their dependency tree as part of their attack surface rather than a separate concern from their own code?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because every dependency runs with exactly the same privileges as the code your team wrote — it can read the same files, hit the same network, and see the same environment variables, including secrets. There's no reduced-trust sandbox separating a third-party package from your own logic in most mainstream runtimes, so a vulnerability in a dependency is functionally identical to one in your own code: same access, same blast radius, same exploitability.

The scale is what makes this a real, not theoretical, problem. A modest number of direct dependencies routinely balloons into hundreds once transitive dependencies are counted — packages your dependencies depend on, which no one on your team explicitly chose or has ever read. A CVE buried three levels deep in that tree is just as usable by an attacker as one in your top-level code, and it's much less likely to be caught by manual review because nobody's manually reading a dependency tree that size.

The practical consequence is that automated scanning (SCA) isn't optional tooling, it's the only mechanism that scales to a dependency tree of that size — manual review of hundreds of transitive packages simply doesn't happen in practice, so if you're not scanning, you effectively have no visibility into most of what's running.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate why dependencies deserve the same scrutiny as first-party code, in terms of actual privilege and access, not just as a vague best practice.

interviewQuestions.question: What does a lockfile actually protect against, and why is reproducibility itself a security property?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A lockfile records the exact resolved version — often down to a specific hash — of every dependency and transitive dependency in a build, instead of the loose version ranges typically declared in a manifest. Without one, two builds from identical source code, run at different times, can resolve to different actual versions if anything in the allowed range was published in between.

That matters for security specifically because it removes an attack window: without a lockfile, a compromised version published into a range you already depend on can get silently pulled into your next build with zero code change on your end — no one on your team did anything wrong, the range itself was just wide enough to let it in. With a lockfile, that same compromised version doesn't get installed until someone deliberately bumps the pinned version, which is a reviewable, visible action rather than an invisible side effect of rebuilding.

The practical discipline that follows: commit the lockfile, and actually look at lockfile diffs during code review — an unexpected new transitive dependency or an unexplained version jump is a real signal, not noise to skim past. Teams that treat the lockfile as an auto-generated file no one reads are giving up exactly the visibility the lockfile exists to provide.

**Testing:** whether you understand reproducibility as closing a real, exploitable window, not just as a convenience for consistent builds.

interviewQuestions.question: A popular open-source package your application depends on has its maintainer account compromised, and a malicious version gets published. Your SCA scanner shows no alerts. Walk me through why, and what you'd do to detect this class of incident.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The SCA scanner shows nothing because it's checking for known, disclosed CVEs — a matched pattern in a vulnerability database. A maliciously published version isn't a coding mistake with an assigned CVE; it's intentional, and it typically ships looking like a completely routine version bump, which is exactly why CVE-based scanning has nothing to match against until, often much later, someone notices the malicious behavior and it gets publicly disclosed and retroactively cataloged.

Detecting this category needs different signals than SCA. I'd want lockfile-diff review as an actual practice, not just a formality — an unusual version jump, a new file type suddenly appearing in a package's contents, or a dependency that unexpectedly gains new transitive dependencies are all worth a second look even without a CVE attached. I'd also want to be deliberate about which dependencies auto-update versus require manual review — a package sitting at the center of your dependency tree with broad blast radius is a better candidate for a pinned, deliberately-reviewed update than an automatic bump on every release.

Beyond the codebase, runtime detection matters here too: outbound network monitoring that would flag a normally-network-quiet library suddenly making unexpected external calls, or unusual reads of environment variables, can catch exactly the kind of exfiltration these incidents typically involve — behavior an SCA scan run at build time can never see, because the malicious behavior only manifests at runtime.

**Testing:** whether you understand the boundary of what SCA covers and can name the different detection layer needed for intentionally malicious, rather than merely vulnerable, dependencies.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Incident response

interviewQuestions.question: As a staff engineer, how would you design your team's dependency update process to avoid both stagnation (never updating, accumulating known CVEs) and the risk of updating everything in one risky batch right before a release?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd aim for a boring, regular cadence, decoupled from release timing entirely — dependency updates happening on their own schedule (weekly or per-PR via an automated bot) rather than being triggered by, or worse, deferred until right before, a release. The goal is that by the time a release approaches, dependencies are already close to current and the release itself doesn't need a dependency-update push at all.

Concretely: automated tooling (Dependabot or similar) opens one PR per dependency update, each reviewed and merged independently rather than batched, so if any single update causes a regression it's immediately isolated to one PR and easy to revert — versus a blanket update where the same regression could be caused by any of forty simultaneously changed packages. I'd have CI gate on SCA findings for new criticals, so a known vulnerability doesn't sit unaddressed just because no one happened to look at a dashboard.

For dependencies with especially broad blast radius — something central to the whole dependency tree, or one flagged in a past incident — I'd apply extra scrutiny before merging an update: reading the actual changelog, not just trusting a green CI run, since CI passing doesn't rule out a supply-chain compromise that behaves identically to the legitimate version in tests. The overall shift I'm going for is turning 'update dependencies' from an occasional, anxiety-inducing event into routine background maintenance that never becomes urgent because it's never allowed to fall far enough behind to be risky.

**Testing:** whether you can design a sustainable process rather than just naming 'update regularly' as an abstract principle without the operational detail that makes it actually work.
